title: Should you buy your kids in-game currency? Here's how we decided
description: Robux, V-Bucks, coins, gems. If you're tired of deciding every single time your kid asks, here's the simple system our family uses instead.
html:
If your kids game, you know the question. "Can I buy some such and such?" It shows up at breakfast, in the car, and right when you sit down for the first time all day. Literally anywhere and anytime.

For a long time I didn't have a real answer, at least not a consistent one. Some days I said yes because I was tired. Some days I said no because I was tired. Neither one felt good, and my kids could tell my answer depended on my mood, not on any rule.

So I want to start with the question a lot of parents quietly ask themselves.

Is it okay to buy your kids in-game currency at all?

I struggled with this a lot. Spending money on game currency felt wasteful in many ways, but after thinking about it, I realized something. Remember being a kid? You asked for stuff too. Trading cards, the candy at the checkout, five more quarters for the arcade. Sometimes your parents said yes.

Robux and V-Bucks are just this generation's version of that. The money isn't really the problem. The problem is that it happens randomly, all the time, with no limit anyone agreed on.

Every ask kicks off a little meeting in your head. Can we afford it this week? Did I already say yes yesterday? Did they do anything to earn it? If I say no, is this about to turn into a meltdown?

One ask is nothing. Ten a week, every week, wears you down. Saying no takes energy. Saying yes takes math.

What changed in our house: decide once

What finally worked for us was moving all of those decisions to one evening. We sat down as a family and agreed on three things:

  1. A monthly limit for each kid. This is the most they can earn in game money in a month. Once it's hit, it's hit.
  2. A points-to-dollars rate. Kids earn points for tasks, and points turn into game money at a rate we set. Ours is simple enough that the kids can do the math themselves.
  3. A payout day. Once a week, points get turned into currency. Not whenever someone asks. Payout day.

Then everyone signed it. Kids too.

Now when someone asks, I don't have to think. I just say, "Check your tracker." If they have the points and it's payout day, great. If not, they know what to do about it.

A few things I learned the hard way

  • Pay on time, every time. If you forget payout day, the whole thing loses its trust fast. If I miss it, the kids get bonus points. That keeps me honest.
  • Don't take away earned points for unrelated stuff. If someone has a rough day, handle that separately. Points they earned stay earned.
  • Let the kids pick some of their tasks. They work a lot harder on jobs they chose.
  • Expect a test in the first week. Most kids push on the new rules once, then settle in after the first payout.

What about gift cards from grandparents?

Decide this ahead of time too, because it will come up. In our house, gift money counts toward the monthly limit unless we agree otherwise for a birthday. Whatever you choose, write it down so nobody has to argue about it in December.

It works with any game that sells in-game currency, and it's $17, one time.

title: How to set up a chore points system your kids will actually stick with
description: A simple points scale, a clear line between everyday jobs and paid ones, and a free printable Earn Menu to get your kids started this week.
html:
I have started a lot of chore charts. Most of them lasted about ten days. The kids were excited, then they weren't, and then the chart was just a piece of paper on the fridge that everyone walked past.

The one that stuck in our house worked for a few simple reasons. None of them are complicated, but skipping any one of them is usually why a chart falls apart.

1. Separate the everyday jobs from the ones that earn

This was the big one for us. Some jobs everyone does just because they live here. Brushing teeth, getting dressed, putting your own plate in the sink. Those don't earn points.

Points go to tasks that take real effort or help the whole family. Without that line, you end up hearing "How many points do I get?" for every little thing, and you'll want to throw the whole chart away.

Sit down and write two lists: family baseline (no points) and Earn Menu (points). That alone clears up a lot.

2. Use a points scale based on time and effort

I tried assigning random numbers to chores once. It turned into constant bargaining. A simple scale ends that, because the rule decides, not me.

Points Effort Example
5 Under 5 minutes Feed the pet, make the bed
10 About 15 minutes Empty the dishwasher, read for 20 minutes
15 to 20 About 30 minutes Vacuum a room, fold all your laundry
25 to 30 An hour or more, or real responsibility Mow the lawn, cook a family dinner

You'll notice reading is on there. As a homeschooling parent, I like that points can reward more than chores. Practicing a skill or finishing a book counts too.

3. Mix daily tasks with bigger weekly ones

A good menu has a few daily tasks, so there's always a way to earn something today, and a few bigger weekly jobs for kids who are saving toward something. Add one or two growth tasks, like reading or practicing an instrument.

4. Let each kid add two tasks of their own

This sounds small, but it changed how my kids treated the whole thing. When they pick a task, it's theirs. They don't need to be reminded nearly as much.

5. Match the tasks to the age

Younger kids, around 6 to 8, need short, simple jobs and quick wins. Kids 9 to 12 can handle bigger jobs and longer saving goals. Teens can take on real-world work and start learning to budget what they earn.

One system can work for every kid in the house. Each one just gets their own menu.

6. Check it once a month

At the end of each month, look at the menu together. Retire tasks that got too easy, raise the stakes as kids grow, and ask what they'd change. Ten minutes is plenty.

title: How we stopped negotiating screen time every night
description: Screen time rules that hold up, even in a homeschool where everyone is home all day. Build the schedule once, agree on consequences while everyone is calm, and stop renegotiating every evening.
html:
When you homeschool, screens are everywhere all day. School happens on a screen sometimes. Free time happens on a screen. And without a clear line between the two, every evening turned into the same conversation in our house. "Five more minutes." "But I didn't get my turn." "You said yesterday I could."

I wasn't against screens. I was against having the same argument every night. Here's what helped.

Build the schedule with your kids, not for them

Kids follow rules they helped write. That's been true in our house for everything, and screen time is no different.

We made three schedules, because one schedule never fits every day:

  • School days. Screens come after the must-dos: schoolwork, tasks, and some time moving or outside.
  • Weekends. More flexible, but still with a start and an end. Family time is protected.
  • Summer. Long days need more structure, not less.

Each one has a daily limit and a "screens off by" time. Once it's on paper, the answer to "can I play?" is already written down.

Pick screen-free zones and a parking spot

We picked a few places where screens just don't go, like the dinner table and bedrooms at night. Then we picked one spot where devices park at the end of the day.

The rule that made this work: it applies to parents too. My kids notice everything, and they notice when my phone is at the table.

Agree on consequences while everyone is calm

This is the part most people skip, and it's the part that saves the most energy. Decide ahead of time what happens if someone goes over or sneaks a device. Write it down as a short ladder, from a reminder up to losing screens for a day.

When it's agreed in advance, you're not making up a punishment in the middle of a meltdown. You're just pointing to what everyone already signed off on.

Keep screen time and game money separate

If your kids game, you'll probably also hear about in-game purchases. I'd keep those as two different systems. Screen time is about when and how long. Game money is about earning and spending. Mixing them makes both harder to enforce. We use The Gaming Money Truce for the money side.

Check in once a month

Once a month we look at the schedule together. What's working, what isn't, what needs to change as the kids get older. We also use that time for a short family lesson about screens or money. Ten minutes is enough.

title: Should you pay kids for chores they're supposed to do anyway?
description: Some jobs are just part of living in a family. Others are worth paying for. Here's how we draw the line, and how to explain it to your kids.
html:
This question comes up every time I talk to another parent about chores. Should kids get paid for helping around the house? Or are some things just what you do because you live here?

I've gone back and forth on it. Where I landed is: both.

The case against paying for everything

If every job earns something, kids learn that helping is a transaction. You ask them to carry in groceries and the first answer is "What do I get?" I don't want my kids to think the family runs on a price list.

There's also a practical problem. If you pay for everything, you'll either go broke or start cutting rates, and then you're back to arguing.

The case for paying for some things

On the other hand, real money skills come from earning real money. A kid who earns, saves for something, and finally buys it learns more than a kid who gets handed the same thing. Earning also gives them a way to get what they want without begging, and that's good for everyone.

And honestly, some jobs are above and beyond. Mowing the lawn or cooking dinner for the family is real work. It's fair to treat it that way.

Where we draw the line

In our house, jobs fall into two lists.

Family jobs (no pay). These are the things everyone does because they're part of this family. Making your bed. Putting your plate in the sink. Picking up your own stuff. Getting your schoolwork done. Nobody gets paid for these, including me.

Earn jobs (points). These are tasks that take real effort or help the whole family beyond the basics. Emptying the dishwasher, vacuuming a room, folding everyone's laundry, cooking a meal. Reading or practicing a skill can go here too.

A simple test I use: if this job didn't get done, would the house still basically work? If the answer is no, it's probably a family job. If the answer is yes, but life is better when it's done, it can be an earn job.

What about when they skip family jobs?

Family jobs come first. In our house, earn jobs don't count until the family jobs are done for the day. That one rule stops kids from skipping their bed to go vacuum for points.

One thing I don't do: take away points they already earned because of an unrelated problem. If someone has a bad attitude at dinner, I deal with that separately. Earned is earned. Otherwise the whole system stops feeling fair.

How to explain it to your kids

Keep it short. Something like:

"Everybody in this family helps, because we live here together. Those jobs aren't paid. If you want to earn something extra, here's the list of jobs you can choose from and what each one is worth."

Then let them help write the earn list. Kids take it more seriously when some of the jobs are their idea.

Write both lists down

The biggest difference for us was putting the two lists on paper where everyone could see them. No more debating in the moment.

title: How much do kids really spend on in-game currency? What the numbers say
description: Robux, V-Bucks, coins and skins add up fast. Here's what surveys say about kids' in-game spending, plus a simple way to see what it costs your family in a year.
html:
Game spending is easy to underestimate. Five dollars here, ten dollars there. It only looks big when you add it up.

If you've ever wondered whether your family spends more than most, or whether you're the only one who gets surprised by a charge, here's what the numbers actually say.

Games are a $60 billion thing in the US

Americans spent $60.7 billion on video games in 2025, according to the Entertainment Software Association and Circana. That's the second-highest year on record. Most of it isn't consoles. It's content: games, add-ons, and in-game purchases.

Kids are a big part of that. They don't always spend the money themselves, but they are very good at asking for it.

In-game currency is the top gift kids ask for

When the ESA asked 700 US kids ages 5 to 17 what they wanted for the 2025 holidays, in-game currency came out on top. 43% asked for it, more than asked for a new console (39%) or a physical game (37%).

So if your kids want Robux or V-Bucks instead of toys this year, you're in very normal company.

A lot of parents find out after the fact

In a survey of about 2,000 US parents of kids ages 6 to 15 by SellCell, 41% said their kids had made in-app purchases without their knowledge. Two out of three said they worried about their kids overspending.

Among parents who did allow purchases, about 4 in 10 kept it to $10 a month or less. On the other end, about 8% said their kids spent more than $100 a month.

That survey is from 2020, but the problem hasn't gone away. In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission ordered the maker of Fortnite to pay $245 million in refunds. One of the FTC's complaints was that kids could rack up charges without a parent being involved.

Most families already have some kind of plan

This is the part I found most encouraging. A 2024 Ipsos survey of 2,772 parents in Europe for Video Games Europe found that most families had an agreement with their kids about in-game spending (73%). Among kids who did spend, the average was €31 a month, down from €39 the year before.

That survey is European, so the numbers won't match the US exactly. But it lines up with what I've seen at home. When the rules are written down, spending gets more predictable.

Do the math for your own family

Small amounts feel small because they come one at a time. Try adding it up for a year:

If your kid spends Per year
$5 a week $260
$10 a week $520
$20 a week $1,040

Multiply that by the number of kids who game in your house. That number isn't meant to make anyone feel guilty. It's just easier to set a limit once you can see it.

What I'd do with these numbers

  • Pick a monthly limit for each kid before they ask. It's much easier to agree on a number at the kitchen table than at the checkout screen.
  • Turn on purchase approval on every device and console your kids use, so nothing gets bought without you.
  • Decide how gift cards count. If grandma sends $50 in game money, does it count toward the monthly limit? Decide now.
  • Let them earn it. When kids trade real effort for their game money, they think a lot harder about how they spend it.

title: 12 holiday gift ideas for kids who game (that aren't just another gift card)
description: Gift ideas for gamer kids ages 6 to 15, from stocking stuffers to family experiences, plus how to give in-game currency without it disappearing by New Year's.
html:
If your kid's holiday list is mostly game money, you're not alone. In an Entertainment Software Association survey of 700 US kids, in-game currency was the number one thing kids asked for last holiday season, ahead of consoles and physical games.

Game money is a fine gift. The trouble is it's usually gone in a day. So here's a list of gift ideas that still fit what a gamer kid loves, with a few that last longer than a weekend.

Stocking stuffers

  1. A small game card with a plan. Pair it with a note that says how it can be spent, or tuck it inside a printed family agreement (more on that at the end).
  2. Reward coupons. Printable coupons for things like "pick the movie," "30 extra minutes of gaming," or "skip one chore." Kids love cashing these in, and they cost you almost nothing.
  3. Play money for earning. Printable "game bucks" that kids earn for tasks and trade in on payout day. Younger kids especially like holding something real.
  4. A pixel-art or sticker book from a game they love. Quiet time that still feels like their thing.

Gifts that get them off the couch a little

  1. A strategy board game. If your kid loves building or strategy games, there's a board game in the same spirit. It's a good way to get the whole family at one table.
  2. A LEGO set or building kit. Builders in a game are usually builders in real life too.
  3. A family tournament night. Wrap a homemade "ticket" for a night where the kid picks the game, makes the bracket, and the winner gets a small prize. This one costs nothing and kids remember it.

Gifts that teach something

  1. A beginner coding or game-design kit. For the kid who says "I want to make games when I grow up." There are good kid-friendly options for ages 8 and up. This one is a favorite of mine as a homeschooling parent.
  2. A savings jar or goal tracker. Help them save toward a bigger game or console themselves. It's amazing how much more careful kids are with money they saved up for.
  3. A real-world "job" gift. A certificate for a paid project, like washing the car or helping clean out the garage, at a rate you set.

Bigger gifts

  1. A good headset or controller. If they play a lot, comfort matters. Make sure purchase approval is turned on for any new device before it's wrapped.
  2. A game they can play with you. Kids in that same ESA survey said they want to play more games with their parents. A co-op game you can both play is a gift for you too.

How to give game money so it lasts

If game money is on the list anyway, here's how I'd do it:

  • Decide up front if it counts toward their monthly limit. Holiday and birthday money is where most game-money rules fall apart.
  • Give it in parts. One card for the holiday, and the rest earned over January.
  • Wrap the rules with it. A gift card inside a printed family agreement turns a one-day gift into a system that lasts all year.
